opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that the advice doesn't have to be trusted by the whole public to matter. It has to be used by the people actually making decisions, and leaders already rely heavily on advisors the public has never heard of and might not trust if they had. Think of a president's economic team, intelligence briefings, or the staff who model what a bill will actually do. Most voters aren't evaluating that advice directly. What they evaluate is outcomes: did the economy do well, did the war go badly, did the pandemic response work.

So if AI systems become genuinely better at forecasting consequences, at saying "if you do policy X, here's the likely distribution of results, and here's how confident we are," then a leader who uses that advice has a competitive edge. They make fewer blunders, and over time that shows up in results that voters do care about, even if those voters are skeptical of AI. There's a selection pressure there, similar to how politicians who ignored polling or good economic analysis tended to do worse.

There's also a verification angle. One of the nice things about AI advice is that you can test it. You can check a system's track record on thousands of forecasts and see whether it was well calibrated. That's much harder with a human pundit or a partisan think tank. A leader or their staff can look at that record and say, "This system has been right far more often than our usual sources," even if the public hasn't caught up to that yet.

And AI can help with something leaders often struggle with: understanding what they themselves would endorse on reflection. A lot of bad decisions don't come from leaders having bad values. They come from not foreseeing consequences, being misled by motivated subordinates, or not having time to think things through. An advisor that can say, "Given what you've said you care about, this course of action is likely to backfire, and here's why," can help even a fairly self-interested politician avoid mistakes they'd regret.

Now, public distrust does matter in some ways. If a leader is seen as just doing whatever the machine says, that can be a political liability, and there are real concerns about whose values are embedded in these systems and who controls them. So you'd want transparency, multiple independent systems, and ways for opposition parties, journalists, and civil society to access comparable tools, so the advice can be checked rather than just taken on faith. But the basic case is that better information and better forecasting improve decisions, and the benefits of that can reach people regardless of whether they're enthusiastic about the source.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders and their staff can evaluate an AI system’s track record and compare it with their usual sources, describing oversight by people working for the leader.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says AI advice need only be used by decisionmakers to matter; the public can remain skeptical while leaders change decisions and voters benefit from the results.

r003.rationale: The response discusses better forecasting and avoiding mistakes, but does not explain that AI eases implementation bottlenecks caused by too few trusted, expert people.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that the people actually making decisions, the leaders themselves, are in a position to verify these systems in a way that cuts through generic public distrust. If you're a head of state or a cabinet official and you've been using an AI advisor over a period of months or years, you get to see its track record directly. It told you that this policy would have these effects, and then you got to watch what happened. It predicted how negotiations would go, how an economy would respond, what the other side would do, and you can check those against reality. And crucially, you can compare it to your human advisors, who you also don't trust unconditionally. Leaders are already accustomed to triangulating between advisors with different biases and agendas.

And then there's the point that in competitive situations, the advantage is just very large. If your rivals, whether that's other governments, other parties, other companies, are getting better forecasts, better strategic analysis, better understanding of the consequences of their options, and you're not, you fall behind. So even someone who starts out skeptical faces enormous pressure to adopt these tools once they're clearly superior. We saw a version of this historically with things like intelligence agencies, or even just using statistics and economic modelling in government. There was resistance, but once the edge became apparent, everybody used them.

Now, the public distrust piece matters, but I'd distinguish between two things. One is distrust of the systems being accurate or honest, and the other is distrust of who controls them and whose interests they serve. The second is a legitimate concern, and it's a big part of why I think you want mechanisms like independent evaluation, systems that can be audited, transparency about when and how they're being used in government. But on the first, the nice thing is that accuracy is checkable. If you have AI systems making many, many forecasts and recommendations, you build up a huge body of evidence, and you can have adversarial checks, different systems built by different parties, each scrutinising the others' claims. That's a situation where a leader can rationally update towards trusting the advice even if their constituents haven't gone through that process.

And I'd add that a lot of the improvement doesn't even require the leader to defer on the controversial value questions. Much of bad decision-making in politics is just factual error, poor forecasting, not thinking through second-order effects, or lacking the time to actually engage with the detail. An advisor that fixes those problems, while leaving the choice of goals to the human, can improve things substantially without anyone having to hand over their values to a machine. The leader still decides what they want. They just get a much clearer picture of how to get it and what it will cost.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders can directly check an AI adviser’s track record and compare its predictions with reality, allowing them to oversee and assess it themselves.

r002.rationale: It says leaders can rationally update toward trusting AI advice even if constituents have not, and describes leaders using that advice while retaining the choice of goals.

r003.rationale: The response mentions poor forecasting, factual errors, and limited time, but does not explain that AI eases policy implementation bottlenecks caused by a shortage of trusted, sufficiently expert people.

astra-6.text:
Well, the public doesn’t have to trust an advisor for that advisor to help a leader make better decisions. Most people don’t know who the president’s technical advisors are, let alone understand or endorse their reasoning. What matters is whether the advice helps the person making the decision.

And a political leader has some interests that are served by having accurate information. They’d generally prefer not to preside over an economic collapse, lose a war, or adopt a policy that fails spectacularly. That doesn’t mean their incentives are perfectly aligned with the public’s, but there’s a substantial range of decisions where better understanding would help both.

An AI advisor could say, “Here’s an assumption your plan depends on. Here’s why it might be wrong. Here’s a way to check it, and here’s an alternative that would better achieve your objective.” You don’t necessarily have to trust the AI’s authority if it can give you arguments and evidence that you can independently assess.

Public distrust would still constrain policies that require public support. And better advice doesn’t turn a selfish leader into a benevolent one. But those are different questions from whether leaders could avoid consequential mistakes by having much better analysis available to them.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders can assess AI arguments and evidence themselves, but does not explain that aligned or subordinate people can oversee the advisers.

r002.rationale: It says public distrust is a different question from whether leaders can use better analysis to avoid mistakes, clearly indicating leaders can change decisions without first persuading the public to trust the advice.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss shortages of trusted experts or AI easing policy implementation bottlenecks.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between the public trusting an AI directly and a political leader being able to use it to make better decisions. A president already relies on advisers whose names most voters don’t know, and whose analysis voters couldn’t independently assess. The advice can still be useful if the president has some way to judge its quality.

With AI, you could test that in areas where you get feedback. Does it make accurate forecasts? Does it identify problems with a proposal that subsequently turn out to be real? Can it explain its reasoning in ways that your other advisers can check? You don’t have to accept everything it says to benefit from having another very capable source of analysis.

And a lot of political decisions involve questions about means, even when people disagree about ends. If you want to achieve some policy objective, which approach is likely to work, what will it cost, and what are the likely unintended consequences? Better advice on those questions could improve decisions without resolving political disagreements.

Public distrust would constrain how leaders could use that advice, particularly if following it looked politically costly. But the AI could also help develop arguments and evidence that people can evaluate on their own merits. So the case doesn’t require everyone to defer to the AI as an authority. It requires useful analysis to reach people who can act on it.

r001.rationale: The response says the president and other advisers could assess AI advice, but does not explain that leaders can trust AI because aligned or subordinate people oversee it.

r002.rationale: It says leaders can use AI for better decisions without requiring the public to defer to or trust the AI.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a shortage of trusted experts or explain how AI could ease policy implementation bottlenecks caused by that shortage.
